title: The Draw of Draws
reviewNotes: Montage, captions and native complete later boards reviewed. Begin after ...gxf2 at 166 seconds in the complete ten-piece later diagram: White Kh1/g2 against Kh4/Qf8/c6/d5/f2/g4/g5/h5. The source g3+ forces either Kxg3 or Kh3, both actual stalemates with every pawn retained until the shown capture. Exact draw verification supplies separate finite non-loss strategies for White and Black: White forces these stalemates; Black’s independent Qf4+ responses to Kh2 prevent a White win through complete legal mate/stalemate leaves. This proves the selected root drawn, not merely one sampled stalemate. The earlier eleven-plus-piece bishop fortress, queen captures and knight sacrifice remain outside this proof.
transcript: knight to e4 check. Black cannot take this knight, otherwise bishop to e1 would be a checkmate. But black can ignore the knight, and the only other move available is king to h4, placing the black king inside a safe shelter behind his pawns. But white continues with another brilliant move, knight to g3. Under the right conditions, one bishop is all you need to face a queen. Bishop to b6, and suddenly black realizes that there is no easy way to reach the white king. If you give a check, the bishop runs to g1, and if you keep the queen on the same line, this is actually going to be a stalemate. The bishop is pinned to the king, and the white king has no legal moves, but it's not checkmated, so this would be considered a draw. But what we find is that there is no setup that black can try to achieve with this queen that doesn't allow the bishop to simply come back every single time. Now, black might try to be smart and realize that if he sacrifices the queen for this pawn and avoids the stalemate, he's most likely going to be still completely winning. So, he might try queen takes, king takes, but incredibly, this would actually allow white to win the game by force because all of these black pawns and this black king are completely stuck. So, this allows white to reroute the bishop and then play bishop takes g3 with a checkmate. So, of course black cannot do that. But the other idea would potentially be to sacrifice the queen for the bishop rather than the pawn. But the black king and all of these pawns are completely stuck in place, and this white king alone is going to be enough to stop the two black pawns. So, okay, if we go back to the starting position, black realizes that he cannot capture the white knight right away. Instead, he tries the very precise queen to f8, realizing that if any other move is played, knight to F5 would actually be another surprising checkmate. But this is of no use because white has the absolutely incredible and brilliant bishop to E1, threatening a double check. If you push a pawn, for example, knight F5 is still a checkmate. But wait a second, black can now take the knight. And there [clears throat] is no way for the bishop to reach G1. So black has successfully tricked white, and now there is no drawing setup, right? Not exactly. White has bishop to F2. Such a tiny, yet so brilliant move. The bishop is threatening to run to G1. That cannot be allowed. But of course, if the black queen takes the bishop, this is still going to be a stalemate. But if the pawn takes the bishop, white is going to play pawn to G3. It doesn't matter whether he moves down or takes the pawn. This could be [music] another stalemate, and another draw.
